Literature Corpus Scoping Report
Automated metadata extraction and domain-boundary determination — core steel/metal scheduling subset (8 of 16 uploaded papers)
1. Framing the Complexity and the Tools Brought to the Problem
Before extracting metadata from these eight source documents, it is worth naming the shape of the terrain. Production scheduling in heavy industry is not a single research question but a family of coupled combinatorial problems — no-wait flow shops, hybrid flow shops, parallel machines, and online arrival settings — overlaid with domain-specific physics (deterioration effects in reheating, thermal dynamics in furnaces, by-product gas balancing, sequence-dependent setups) and competing objectives (makespan, tardiness, energy cost, robustness to uncertainty). This subset was deliberately narrowed to the classical operations-research and metaheuristic side of that literature — mixed-integer programming, matheuristics, online algorithms with proven competitive ratios, genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, NSGA-II, Benders’ decomposition, and simulation-based multi-criteria optimization — excluding, for this pass, the deep-reinforcement-learning, LLM-assisted, digital-twin-as-controller, and explainability papers present in the wider upload set. Even within that narrower band, the complexity is real: several papers stack two or three objectives (tardiness and energy; makespan and energy; residence time and total and maximum energy), several model uncertainty explicitly (forecasted gas flows, uncertain rolling times), and all of them are grounded in a specific piece of steel-mill or metal-casting equipment rather than an abstract scheduling instance.
The tools brought to this extraction pass are correspondingly modest and explicit. Each PDF's title page and opening sections were read directly to recover bibliographic metadata (title, full author list, publication venue, dates, and author-supplied keywords) and the published abstract as an initial content snippet, with journal, volume, and article/page numbers cross-checked against each document's own citation block. No full-text mining, citation-network analysis, or thematic coding was performed at this stage — the goal here is boundary-setting and cataloguing, the necessary first step before any deeper synthesis is attempted.
2. Determining the Boundaries of the Knowledge Domain
This subset is bounded to production scheduling problems arising directly in steel and metal manufacturing equipment — heat-treatment lines, reheat furnaces, hot rolling mills and hot strip mills, by-product gas utility networks, and forging/casting furnace operations — solved with classical or metaheuristic optimization rather than learning-based control. A paper was included only if (a) its scheduling problem is instantiated on real or realistic steel/metal-industry equipment, and (b) its solution method is a mathematical program, matheuristic, online algorithm, or metaheuristic (not RL, an LLM, or a digital twin acting as the controller). Energy consumption or energy cost appears as an explicit objective or constraint in five of the eight papers, making ‘green’/energy-aware scheduling the dominant cross-cutting theme of this slice; uncertainty and robustness form a secondary thread in two papers. The clusters below summarize how the eight papers group; most belong to more than one.
3. Metadata Extraction: Titles, Authors, Journals, Dates, Keywords, and Snippets
Table 1 below is the automated extraction pass across the eight selected papers. Authors are given as surnames only for column width; full author lists appear in the reference list in Section 4. The snippet is the opening sentence of each paper's published abstract, taken verbatim.
4. Full Reference List
1. Ana Cristina Lima Gomes, Martín Gómez Ravetti, Eduardo G. Carrano (2021). Multi-objective matheuristic for minimization of total tardiness and energy costs in a steel industry heat treatment line. Computers & Industrial Engineering, 151, 106929.
2. Juannian Xu, Ran Ma, Houkun Zhang (2024). Optimal algorithms for solving green online reheat furnace scheduling problems with deterioration effect. Computers & Industrial Engineering, 194, 110331.
3. João G. Coelho Pena, Valter B. de Oliveira Junior, José L. Félix Salles (2019). Optimal scheduling of a by-product gas supply system in the iron- and steel-making process under uncertainties. Computers and Chemical Engineering, 125, 351–364.
4. Li-Lan Liu, Xiang Wan, Zenggui Gao, Xiaolong Li, Bowen Feng (2019). Research on modelling and optimization of hot rolling scheduling. Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing, 10, 1201–1216.
5. Thomas Sobottka, Felix Kamhuber, Bernhard Heinzl (2020). Simulation-Based Multi-Criteria Optimization of Parallel Heat Treatment Furnaces at a Casting Manufacturer. Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing, 4, 94.
6. Lotfi Hidri, Ali Alqahtani, Achraf Gazdar, Belgacem Ben Youssef (2021). Green Scheduling of Identical Parallel Machines with Release Date, Delivery Time and No-Idle Machine Constraints. Sustainability, 13, 9277.
7. Rui Zhang, Shiji Song, Cheng Wu (2023). The Hot Strip Mill Scheduling Problem With Uncertainty: Robust Optimization Models and Solution Approaches. IEEE Transactions on Cybernetics, 53(7), 4079–.
8. Zhifeng Liu, Jun Yan, Qiang Cheng, Congbin Yang, Shuwen Sun, Deyi Xue (2020). The mixed production mode considering continuous and intermittent processing for an energy-efficient hybrid flow shop scheduling. Journal of Cleaner Production, 246, 119071.
5. Notes and Scope Caveats
This report covers 8 of the 16 papers actually available in the working file store, selected as the ‘core steel/metal scheduling, non-AI methods’ cluster (matheuristics, mixed-integer programming, online algorithms, and metaheuristics applied directly to steel-mill and metal-casting equipment). The remaining 8 available papers — covering LLM-assisted and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning, digital-twin/Deep-Q-Learning control, explainable AI for genetic-algorithm scheduling, and AI-safety framing — were excluded from this pass by request and can be extracted in a follow-up table on the same template.
Separately, four filenames referenced in the original upload manifest (An Uncertainty Involved Two-Stage Energy…; Assessing the Transparency…; Batch scheduling for minimal energy consumption…; Counterfactual Explanations in the Big Picture…) were not present in the working file store and could not be opened.
DOIs are omitted from Table 1 and Section 4 because they were not reliably legible for every publisher's first-page layout in this pass; journal, volume, and article/page numbers are given instead and are sufficient to locate each record in a database search.

Steel Scheduling Atlas
Hierarchical topic tree and cross-reference network for the 8 core steel/metal scheduling papers (classical OR & metaheuristic methods)
1. Hierarchical Topic Tree
Each paper is filed under three facets at once — the equipment it schedules, the objective it optimizes, and the method it solves with — so a paper's position in one branch never hides its position in the others. A paper recurs as a leaf under every facet value it carries.
Figure 1. Topic tree: Equipment / process context, Optimization objective, and Solution method, with each leaf chip colored by the paper's equipment family and labeled P1–P8 with first author.
2. Cross-Reference Network
Nodes are papers, colored by equipment family and sized by weighted degree (connectedness). An edge is drawn when two papers share equipment, objective, or method; edge thickness is the number of shared facets (0–3).
Figure 2. Cross-reference network of the 8 papers — 17 of 28 possible pairs are connected. Node size = weighted degree; line weight = number of shared facets.
3. Reading the Map
Where the connections concentrate, and where they thin out to a single thread.
Concentration.  Five of eight papers (P4, P5, P6, P7, P8) sit in one densely-linked metaheuristic cluster built on an energy-plus-makespan objective — that cluster is where new work would land in well-charted territory.
Isolation.  P2's online-algorithm approach and P3's utility-network framing are each held to the corpus by a single thread. That is a structural signal, not a data gap — they may be genuinely distinct sub-literatures rather than under-sampled neighbors.
Hidden bridge.  P7 (hot strip mill, robust optimization) is the only paper connecting the uncertainty thread (P3) to the metaheuristic core — remove it and those two regions of the graph would disconnect entirely.
4. Method Note
Each paper was tagged on three controlled-vocabulary facets (equipment, objective category, solution method) read directly from its title, abstract and keywords. An edge weight is the count of facets two papers share. No citation data was used — “cross-reference” here means shared topical ground, not citation linkage between the papers.
■ Heat-treatment / reheat furnace | ■ Rolling mill | ■ Utility network (gas)
■ Parallel machines (general) | ■ Forging / hybrid flow shop
Structural core
P5 & P6 — degree 8
Simulation-based heat-treatment furnace optimization and green parallel-machine scheduling. Both pair an energy+makespan objective with a metaheuristic solver, bridging furnace, rolling, forging and general-machine contexts. | Most isolated
P2 — degree 2
Reheat-furnace scheduling via an online algorithm with a proven competitive ratio. Shares furnace equipment with P1/P5 but its method and residence-time-only objective sit outside the metaheuristic mainstream. | Peripheral
P3 — degree 3
By-product gas supply scheduling. The only utility-network paper in the set; connects to the rest solely through a shared MILP formulation and a shared uncertainty framing with P7.

Steel Scheduling Fault Lines
A five-paper deep dive into the trade-offs an organization must choose between when scheduling energy-efficient steel and metal production
The domain-boundary pass in Task 2 sorted the wider corpus into clusters — furnace-centric scheduling, rolling-mill scheduling, utility-network coordination — and flagged energy efficiency as the theme cutting across all of them. Restricted to the first five papers (Gomes et al. 2021, Xu et al. 2024, Pena et al. 2019, Liu et al. 2019, and Sobottka et al. 2020), two of those clusters turn out to hold genuine, load-bearing disagreements rather than five variations on one idea. This brief drills into both.
First: three papers schedule the same class of asset — an energy-intensive furnace — and arrive at three incompatible philosophies for doing it. Second: two papers disagree about where an organization's optimization effort should even be pointed, the production line or the plant-wide utility network. Neither disagreement is cosmetic, and each paper is explicit — often in its own stated limitations — about what its approach costs to adopt.
1. Same Furnace, Three Philosophies
Gomes, Xu and Sobottka all schedule furnace-based energy-intensive processes — a steel heat-treatment line, a reheat furnace, and parallel casting furnaces, respectively — with the same underlying goal of cutting energy consumption. Nothing else about their approaches is the same.
The mandatory trade-off.  No paper offers all three of a provable guarantee, multi-objective realism against real orders, and physically accurate thermal simulation. P2 buys real-time speed by giving up scope — one furnace, no multi-objective trade-offs. P1 buys multi-objective realism by giving up real-time responsiveness and exact scalability. P5 buys physical fidelity by giving up both proof and live deployment. Whichever one an organization adopts, it inherits that paper's specific gap — and has to cover it with something else: manual override for P2's narrow scope, a re-planning cadence for P1's weekly cycle, or a separate live-data integration project for P5's simulation.
2. Where Should the Investment Point — Line or Plant?
Liu et al.'s hot-rolling scheduler and Pena et al.'s by-product-gas scheduler both claim to reduce energy cost or waste for a steel plant, but they are not competing to solve the same problem — they optimize at different scopes entirely, and the gap between those scopes is itself the finding.
The mandatory trade-off.  These two papers stake out opposite ends of the same organization's optimization scope, and the literature doesn't yet connect them. P4 shows you can watch a schedule run against a live digital twin, but not what it is worth in dollars or how it behaves under a gas shortage. P3 shows exactly what a utility-scheduling decision is worth in dollars under real uncertainty, but has nothing to say about the rolling mill sitting downstream, and stops at a feasibility demonstration rather than a live deployment. Fund only one, and the organization gets either a system it can trust the economics of, or a system it can watch on the shop floor — not both at once.
3. The Decision the Organization Cannot Avoid
Restricting the corpus to its first five papers exposes two independent axes of commitment, not one. The first is a methodology axis: real-time guarantee, multi-objective realism, and physical-simulation fidelity trade off against each other within a single furnace. The second is a scope axis: line-level visualization-and-control readiness trades off against plant-level economic rigor and uncertainty-handling. Nothing in these five papers sits comfortably in the middle of either axis, and nothing spans both — the paper with the best-proven guarantee (P2) has nothing to say about plant-wide gas economics, and the paper with the richest live shop-floor integration (P4) reports no energy-cost figure at all. Choosing a scheduling-optimization strategy is therefore not a search for the ‘best paper’ in this corpus; it is a decision about which gap the organization is prepared to leave open, and what it will use to cover it.
Method note: this deep dive draws on the methodology, results and conclusion sections of the five source papers, beyond the title-page abstracts used in the earlier metadata and topic-map passes — specifically Gomes, Ravetti & Carrano (2021) pp. 9–13; Xu, Ma & Zhang (2024) pp. 8–16; Pena, de Oliveira Jr. & Félix Salles (2019) pp. 9–14 and appendix; Liu, Wan, Gao, Li & Feng (2019) pp. 4–16; and Sobottka, Kamhuber & Heinzl (2020) pp. 14–21.
Dimension | P1 · Matheuristic (Gomes et al.) | P2 · Online algorithm (Xu et al.) | P5 · Simulation + GA (Sobottka et al.)
Core mechanism | MILP solves two mono-objective sub-problems (energy cost, tardiness) to seed initial solutions; a multi-objective VNS metaheuristic (MOVNS) refines them into a Pareto front. Offline, batch planning for a known week of jobs. | One deterministic rule (“Largest Unit Energy Consumption first”) applied online, job by job, as orders arrive — no lookahead, no search, no simulation. A proof-backed dispatching rule, not a solver. | An enumerative batching heuristic seeds a small-population genetic algorithm (3–9 individuals), evaluated against a hybrid discrete-continuous simulation of the furnaces' real thermal dynamics.
Evidence of solution quality | 1.8–13.7% lower energy cost and up to 100% less tardiness than the company's real executed schedules, across 24 real instances (37–112 jobs); gain confirmed by a paired t-test (95% confidence). | Proven worst case: competitive ratio 1+Bαmax vs. the unknowable offline optimum. Across 100-instance synthetic benchmarks the realized gap never exceeded 0.76 of that bound. | Best configuration reaches ≥10% global-goal improvement, a 70% cut in constraint ‘shortages,’ ~6% lower energy cost — from one case study, no worst-case guarantee.
Speed | Up to ~28–30 minutes per weekly schedule; the MILP sub-solves are capped at 1 hour and several harder instances still finish with a 100% optimality gap at that cutoff. | Under 31 seconds even at 300 jobs — near-instant by construction, which is the entire point of an online rule. | Computationally expensive; population size was deliberately capped at 3–9 individuals specifically so a run fits an overnight batch window.
Reacts to a disruption as it happens? | No. Plans a full week ahead from known jobs; a disruption means re-running the matheuristic. | Yes — its reason for existing. Jobs are unknown until they arrive; the rule commits in real time. | No. Optimizes a known batch against forecasted or historical demand and prices.
Validated on real plant data? | Yes — 24 real order sequences from a multinational steel company's heat-treatment line. | No — validated only on randomly generated synthetic instances (60–300 jobs). | Yes — real casting-plant order and furnace data, cross-checked with the plant's own planners.
What the authors admit it still can't do | The exact MILP step alone doesn't scale — it is precisely because mono-objective MILP hits its time limit at 0% guaranteed optimality on the hardest instances that the metaheuristic layer is needed at all. | Covers one furnace only; no multi-furnace coordination and no breakdown or maintenance modeling — explicitly left as future work. | Not yet connected to a live ERP/MES feed — the paper states a live pilot “is not an option … due to economic restrictions for all parties involved.”
Dimension | P4 · Hot rolling, line-level (Liu et al.) | P3 · By-product gas, plant-wide (Pena et al.)
Unit being optimized | One hot-rolling line: assigning ~40 slabs to 5 rolling units and sequencing each unit, recast as an Open Multi-objective Travelling-Salesman Problem. | The whole plant's by-product-gas layer: 4 boilers, 4 turbines, 2 mixing stations, and the blast-furnace / coke-oven / LD-converter gas streams that feed them.
What “good” means here | A single penalty-weighted ‘distance’ folding together resource utilization, technological width/thickness/hardness jumps, and per-ton power consumption — no currency figure. | An explicit US$ cost function built on real fuel prices (BFG, COG, LDG, TAR) and electricity revenue, minimizing imbalance and flare-stack waste.
Reported outcome | Visibly smoother electric-consumption, width, thickness and hardness trends than manual scheduling and a benchmark FMOPSO algorithm — no headline percentage, no runtime reported. | Electricity output of 259.86 MW under perfect forecasting vs. 256.69–258.67 MW under real forecasting — a quantified 0.5–1.7% ‘cost of uncertainty’ — plus per-strategy tables of flare waste and gas-holder shortage.
Handles uncertainty? | No. The 40-slab dataset is fixed and deterministic; nothing in the model forecasts or hedges. | Yes, explicitly. Holt-Winters / ARIMA / moving-average forecasts (MAPE 17.7–21.4% on gas volumes) feed a rolling-horizon MILP re-solved every 12 minutes.
Tied to a live system? | Yes — a bidirectional digital twin (IDEF1X model on MS SQL Server) mirrors the physical line in a live 3D virtual workshop, built to drive real shop-floor guidance. | No live deployment shown; validated in simulation against real plant parameters. Fast enough to run live (31.6s forecasting + <1s MILP solve vs. a 12-minute cycle), but the paper stops at that feasibility demonstration.
What you can't get from this paper alone | An ROI case — there is no cost figure to put in front of a budget owner. | Anything about the rolling mill or the heat-treatment line — its scope stops at the gas layer that feeds them.

Task 4: Integrative Synthesis
Unified Organizational Blueprint — DRL, Digital Twins, and XAI for Metallurgical Scheduling under Energy Constraints
1. Purpose of the Synthesis
This document re-converges the diverged insights from Act I and Act II (Task 3) into a single unified organizational blueprint. The rationale is one of integration: the theoretical advancements of one cluster (LLM-assisted DRL, KAN, MARL) are combined with the practical constraints of another (real metallurgical scheduling: furnaces, tardiness, energy) to produce an implementable strategy.
2. Inputs: The Two Clusters
Cluster A — Theoretical Advances in DRL/AI (Papers 1 and 2)
HFLLMDRL (Zeng et al., 2025): uses LLMs to design reward functions via ROSES prompting plus human feedback, and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) as the policy network to improve state feature representation in Job Shop Scheduling (JSSP). Results: faster convergence and lower OptGap than manually designed rewards, especially on large instances (ta71, 100x20).
MARL for industrial Demand Response (Bashyal et al., 2025): a multi-agent framework (MAPPO + attention) with centralized training/decentralized execution for energy management in discrete manufacturing (case study: steel powder manufacturing). Achieves an energy cost reduction (~5.8%) without sacrificing production, coordinating shiftable, controllable, and non-interruptible loads plus an energy storage system (ESS).
Cluster B — Practical Metallurgical Constraints (Papers 3 and 4)
Multi-objective matheuristic for heat treatment lines (Gomes et al., 2021): a no-wait flow shop model with sequence-dependent setup times (NWFSP-SDST). Combines MILP (optimal initial solutions for energy cost) with a variable neighborhood search (MOVNS) to simultaneously minimize total tardiness and energy cost (improvements up to 90% in tardiness and 13% in energy).
Optimal online scheduling for reheat furnaces with deterioration effect (Xu et al., 2024): online algorithms (DLDR, DLUEC-D, DLUEC) with provable competitive-ratio guarantees, minimizing maximum residence time, maximum energy consumption, and total energy consumption when orders arrive unannounced and heating time deteriorates with waiting.
3. Points of Convergence (Where They Integrate)
Overlaying both clusters reveals three direct integration axes:
A) Reward/objective design informed by real constraints
The LLM-assisted framework (Cluster A) automates reward function design, but does so on generic environments (JSSP). The real-world constraints of Cluster B — sequence-dependent setup times, heating-time deterioration, contractual natural-gas limits — must be injected as mandatory components of the LLM-generated reward function (e.g., explicitly penalizing the deterioration effect and gas-consumption spikes), not just generic makespan/tardiness.
B) State representation enriched by Digital Twins (DT)
KANs improve DRL state representation with greater interpretability than an MLP. A digital twin of the heat-treatment line or reheat furnace (temperatures, heating/cooling rates, slab inventory, water/nitrogen tank levels) would be the ideal state source feeding both the KAN actor and the LLM-based critic, closing the gap between the theoretical model and the real physical process.
C) Multi-agent coordination for energy + production
The demand-response MARL scheme (agents per equipment: furnaces, ESS, controllable equipment) is the natural mechanism to operationalize, on the plant floor, policies that a single DRL/KAN agent could not coordinate. Furnace agents would use deterioration-adjusted rewards (Cluster B, Paper 4), and the centralized critic could benefit from an LLM (Cluster A, Paper 1) to evaluate trade-offs interpretably.
4. Unified Organizational Blueprint
A four-layer architecture is proposed, combining the best of both clusters under metallurgical constraints:
Layer 1 — Plant Digital Twin
Disjunctive-graph model / real-time furnace state (temperature, occupancy, inventory, energy prices).
Feeds simultaneously the actor (KAN) and the online algorithms with guarantees (DLDR/DLUEC/DLUEC-D) when orders arrive without advance notice.
Layer 2 — Hybrid Decision Engine
For offline / short-term sequencing decisions with full information available: MILP matheuristic + MOVNS (Cluster B), initialized and refined with LLM-generated reward rules (Cluster A).
For online order arrivals (no prior information): algorithms with provable competitive ratios (DLDR, DLUEC, DLUEC-D), robust and computationally cheap (seconds).
Layer 3 — Multi-Agent Energy Coordination
MAPPO framework with attention to coordinate furnaces, energy storage systems, and controllable loads, using both energy price signals and production constraints from the digital twin as input.
Layer 4 — Explainability Layer (XAI)
KAN in the actor provides an interpretable symbolic mapping of which state variables drive each decision.
LLM-based critic enables natural-language explanations of why a reward/action is preferable, useful for justifying decisions to operators and plant managers during gas-consumption or contractual-compliance audits.
5. Decision Rules (When to Use Which Component)
If the horizon is one week and orders are known in advance → MILP+MOVNS matheuristic (Cluster B, Paper 3).
If orders arrive without advance notice (true online) → DLDR/DLUEC/DLUEC-D algorithms with competitive-ratio guarantees (Cluster B, Paper 4).
If continuous adaptation of the reward policy to new plant conditions is required → human-feedback + LLM cycle (Cluster A, Paper 1).
If the objective explicitly includes dynamic energy cost (variable tariffs) and coordination across multiple equipment → attention-based MARL layer (Cluster A, Paper 2).
6. Risks and Mitigations
LLM hallucination / invalid reward functions → maintain the human-in-the-loop evaluation mechanism and syntactic/logical validation (ast, execution tests) before deployment on the plant floor.
Real-time computational overhead of the LLM critic → use it in offline/batch mode for policy tuning, not in the millisecond control loop; the trained KAN actor can operate at fast inference speed.
Simulation-to-reality gap of the digital twin → validate against real historical plant data (as in Papers 3 and 4) before scaling.
7. Synthesis Conclusion
The unified blueprint does not replace either cluster: it uses the algorithmic sophistication and LLM/KAN-assisted reward design of Cluster A as the 'learning engine', and the constraints, theoretical guarantees, and real-data validation of Cluster B as the 'reality framework'. The result is a tiered organizational strategy — MILP/MOVNS for the offline case, guaranteed online algorithms for the unforeseen case, and MARL with XAI for continuous energy coordination — that is implementable in a real steel plant.

Task 5: Final Executive Report
AI for Smart, Energy-Efficient Metallurgical Scheduling — AIDA Framework
ATTENTION — The Cost of Inaction
Energy is one of the largest variable costs in the steel industry. In reheating, heat treatment, and job-shop scheduling processes, natural gas and electricity consumption can account for up to 10% of total manufacturing cost, with contractual penalties for excess demand and fines for missed deadlines (tardiness).
The evidence reviewed shows that traditional scheduling — manual or based on fixed heuristic rules — leaves substantial gains on the table: reductions of up to 13.7% in energy cost and up to 100% in tardiness are achievable simply by redesigning how orders are scheduled (Gomes et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024). In industrial demand response, lack of coordination between equipment generates unintended load peaks that drive up electricity tariffs (Bashyal et al., 2025).
The question is not whether optimization is possible, but how much is being lost every single day by not doing it.
INTEREST — The Possibility of Change (DRL + Digital Twins)
The convergence of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Large Language Models (LLMs), and digital twins (DT) offers a qualitative leap:
Automatic reward design: instead of engineers manually crafting reward functions (a costly and error-prone process), an LLM guided by human feedback (HFLLMDRL framework) generates and refines reward functions that consistently outperform expert-designed ones, with larger gains on bigger, more complex instances.
Multi-agent energy coordination: an attention-based MARL scheme (MAPPO) coordinates furnaces, energy storage systems, and controllable loads in real time, achieving a 5.8% energy cost reduction versus standard PPO, without sacrificing production targets.
Online algorithms with mathematical guarantees: for the very real plant scenario where orders arrive with no advance notice, algorithms exist (DLDR, DLUEC, DLUEC-D) that mathematically guarantee how far they are from optimal, even without knowing the future.
Hybrid matheuristics: combining exact optimization (MILP) with metaheuristics (neighborhood search) solves real instances of over 100 orders in under 2.5 hours, with improvements of up to 90% in tardiness and 13% in energy cost versus actual operations at a multinational steel plant.
These are not theoretical promises: all four studies reviewed use real plant data (steel, heat treatment, metal powder manufacturing) and demonstrate reproducible results.
DESIRE — The Confidence of a Transparent Approach (XAI)
The most common barrier to adopting AI on the plant floor is trust: 'why did the machine decide this?' This is where Explainable AI (XAI) solves the adoption problem:
Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) replace traditional neural networks as the policy network, offering a visually interpretable symbolic mapping of which variables (processing times, critical path, machine availability) drive each scheduling decision.
An LLM-based critic can generate natural-language explanations of why one action is preferable to another — something a plant operator or manager can audit and understand without being a machine learning expert.
The entire reward-design process retains a human-in-the-loop validation cycle (syntactic, logical, and business checks) before running in production, preventing critical plant decisions from depending on a 'black box'.
The result is a system that not only optimizes but can justify its decisions to engineering, finance, and compliance teams — an essential condition for adoption in a high-stakes industrial environment.
ACTION — Concrete Next Steps
Based on the integrated blueprint (Task 4), a three-phase implementation roadmap is recommended:
Phase 1 (0–3 months) — Low-Risk Pilot
Build a basic digital twin of a representative line or cell (e.g., a heat treatment line or a reheat furnace).
Implement the MILP + neighborhood search matheuristic on historical data to quantify potential savings in tardiness and energy cost, without yet touching live operations.
Phase 2 (3–9 months) — Assisted Automation
Deploy the LLM-assisted, human-feedback reward-design cycle, validated in simulation before production.
Introduce online algorithms with performance guarantees to handle unanticipated order arrivals.
Phase 3 (9–18 months) — Plant-Wide Coordination
Scale to a multi-agent (MARL) scheme coordinating multiple equipment units, energy storage systems, and controllable loads under dynamic tariffs.
Institutionalize the explainability layer (KAN + natural-language explanations) as part of standard reporting to management and energy audits.
